question: like God, or like gods / divine beings
context: Elohim earlier in the verse is God, and the serpent promises a share in God's own knowledge; 3:22 'like one of us' confirms divine knowledge, though its plural leaves room for the heavenly council. The plural participle yod'e fits either reading. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV and CSB have 'like God'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'like gods' — LXX hos theoi, Vulgate sicut dii, KJV; (2) 'like divine beings', i.e. members of the heavenly council (cf. 3:22 'one of us') — NJPS, NET; (3) 'like great ones/princes' — Targum Onkelos, avoiding a direct comparison with God.

question: Nephilim: a name, 'giants' or 'fallen ones'
verdict: keep the name Nephilim; remembered as huge
context: Nephilim is a term of uncertain meaning, best transliterated, as ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS, CSB and NET do. Num 13:33 links them with the gigantic Anakim, so 'giants' reflects how Israel remembered them, but rendering 'giants' turns an interpretation into the word's meaning. Other possible meanings: (1) 'giants' — LXX gigantes, Vulgate, KJV, supported by Num 13:33 and later Jewish tradition (1 Enoch, Jubilees); (2) 'fallen ones' (from naphal) — Genesis Rabbah and some modern scholars, sometimes linked with fallen angels; (3) 'assailants/violent ones' — Aquila (epipiptontes), Symmachus (biaioi); (4) 'mighty men' — Targum Onkelos (gibbaraya).

question: Asshur went out, or he (Nimrod) went out to Assyria
context: 10:8-12 is a single unit on Nimrod's kingdom, Asshur son of Shem appears only at 10:22, and Mic 5:6 calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod'; a bare accusative of destination after yatsa' is possible. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, CSB and NET read Nimrod. But every ancient version makes Asshur the subject, so confidence is lowered from high to medium. Other possible meanings: (1) 'Asshur went out (from that land) and built Nineveh', Asshur being a person, ancestor of the Assyrians — LXX, Vulgate, Targum Onkelos, Josephus, KJV, NJPS; (2) the same, with Asshur as the Assyrian people migrating from Babylonia — some commentators.

question: test, or tempt
context: Nissah means to test or prove (Exod 16:4; Deut 8:2); 22:12 'now I know that you fear God' states the aim, a test of loyalty, not enticement to sin (Jas 1:13). All major modern translations have 'tested' (NJPS 'put Abraham to the test'). Other possible meanings: (1) 'tempted' — KJV, following Vulgate tentavit and LXX epeirazen, which in their day could mean 'test'; in modern English it implies enticing to sin, which the text does not mean; (2) 'proved' — Geneva Bible; same sense as 'tested'.

question: nations 'be blessed' (passive) or 'bless themselves' (reflexive)
verdict: find blessing (keeps passive and reflexive senses open)
context: The hithpael hitbarakhu (as 22:18) is normally reflexive, 'bless themselves' (cf. 48:20), but the parallel promises use the niphal (12:3; 18:18; 28:14), the hithpael can carry middle/passive force, and LXX, Vulgate and the NT (Acts 3:25; Gal 3:8) read 'be blessed'. The evidence is balanced; 'find blessing' keeps both senses. Other possible meanings: (1) 'shall be blessed' (receive blessing through the offspring) — LXX eneulogethesontai, Vulgate benedicentur, Acts 3:25, Gal 3:8, KJV, ESV, NIV, NASB, CSB; (2) 'shall bless themselves by' (invoke the offspring as a model of blessing, cf. 48:20) — NJPS, NET ('pronounce blessings ... using the name'), NRSV ('gain blessing for themselves'), many critical commentators.

question: coat of many colours, or long robe with sleeves
context: Ketonet passim recurs only in 2 Sam 13:18-19, a princess's garment, so it marks status. Pas 'palm/sole' suggests a robe reaching to wrists and ankles, as Aquila, Symmachus and the LXX of 2 Sam 13:18 (karpotos) took it; but the LXX here and a proposed Akkadian parallel point to colour or ornament. The meaning is genuinely uncertain; confidence lowered. Other possible meanings: (1) 'a coat of many colours / multicolored tunic' — LXX chitona poikilon, Vulgate polymitam, KJV, ESV, NASB; (2) 'an ornate/ornamented robe' (embroidered or with appliqué) — NIV, NJPS, cf. Akkadian kitu pisannu; (3) 'a special tunic', leaving the feature unstated — NET; (4) a tunic of fine wool — Rashi.

question: habitations, or swords
context: Mekheroteihem is a hapax. 'Swords/blades' (perhaps related to Greek machaira, as Rashi already noted) fits the recollection of Gen 34:25, where Simeon and Levi 'took their swords', and is the reading of ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, CSB and NET. The derivation remains uncertain. Other possible meanings: (1) 'their habitations / land of sojourning' (from gur) — Targum Onkelos, KJV; (2) 'their origin/kinship' (cf. mekhorah, Ezek 16:3) — some medieval and modern interpreters; (3) 'their schemes' (from karah 'plot') — LXX ex haireseos auton ('of their own choice'), some commentators; (4) 'their weapons' generally — NJPS.

question: Shiloh (place or name), or 'he to whom it belongs'
verdict: until he comes to whom it belongs
context: Reading shello 'whose it is' has the widest ancient support: Ezek 21:32 (Eng 21:27) 'until he comes whose right it is', LXX (ta apokeimena auto / ho apokeitai), Symmachus, Peshitta and the Targums ('until Messiah comes, whose is the kingdom'). The parallel 'the obedience of the peoples is his' needs a person. NIV and NET agree. Other possible meanings: (1) 'until Shiloh comes', a personal (messianic) name — KJV, NASB, Talmud (Sanh 98b), Genesis Rabbah; (2) 'until tribute comes to him' (shay lo) — ESV, NRSV, NJPS; (3) 'until he comes to Shiloh' (the town) — some medieval and critical scholars; (4) 'until his ruler comes' (Akkadian shelu) — a few modern scholars. Also 'gathering' (KJV) for yiqqehat 'obedience'.

question: God was not 'known' by the name Yahweh, though Genesis uses it
verdict: known in the character the name expresses
context: Genesis uses the name Yahweh, even in God's speech to the patriarchs (15:7; 28:13). In 6:6-7 'you shall know that I am Yahweh' means experiencing the name through redemption, so the contrast is one of revelation, not vocabulary. The rendering keeps the Hebrew open; the KJV difference is only the form of the name. Other possible meanings: (1) the name itself was unknown before Moses, and Genesis uses it anachronistically — many source-critical scholars (assigning 6:3 to P); (2) a rhetorical question, 'by my name Yahweh did I not make myself known to them?' — a minority of interpreters; (3) the patriarchs received the promises but not their fulfilment, which the name signifies — Rashi.

question: I will praise him, or prepare him a habitation
context: The parallel 'I will exalt him' and the LXX (doxaso) and Vulgate (glorificabo) favour 'praise/glorify' (from naweh 'be beautiful, fitting'), as nearly all major translations render. But naveh 'abode' recurs in the same song (15:13, 17), so the Targum's 'build him a sanctuary' is a real possibility; confidence lowered from high to medium. Other possible meanings: (1) 'I will prepare him a habitation / enshrine him' (from naveh 'abode') — Targum Onkelos, KJV, NJPS ('enshrine Him'); (2) 'I will adorn him', honouring him with beautiful worship — Mekhilta, Rashi; (3) 'I will be like him' (ani wahu) — Abba Shaul in Mekhilta and Talmud (Shab 133b).

question: hand upon the throne of Yah (oath), or upon the banner of Yah
verdict: A hand upon the throne of Yah
context: MT kes is most simply a short form of kisse' 'throne'; the Samaritan Pentateuch reads ks', and the Vulgate (solii) and Targums read 'throne'. 'Banner' requires emending kes to nes, attractive after v.15 (Yahweh-nissi) but unsupported by any witness. ESV, NIV, NJPS, CSB and NET read 'throne'. Whose hand, raised in oath or against the throne, is left open. Other possible meanings: (1) 'a hand upon the banner of Yah' (emending to nes, cf. 17:15) — NRSV, many critical commentators; (2) an oath, 'Yahweh has sworn' (hand raised upon the throne) — Targum, Rashi, KJV, NASB95; (3) Amalek's hand raised against Yahweh's throne — NIV; (4) 'with a hidden hand' (from ksh 'cover') — LXX.

question: bring him to God, or to the judges
context: Ha'elohim is normally 'God'; 22:7-8 uses the same phrase for a verdict, there with a plural verb, which some take as 'judges'. The rite at the door may be at the sanctuary or the household doorpost. ESV, NASB, NRSV and NJPS read 'God'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'to the judges' — Targum Onkelos, Rashi, KJV, NIV, CSB, NET, taking elohim as judges acting for God (cf. Ps 82:6); (2) 'to the tribunal of God' — LXX pros to kriterion tou theou; (3) 'to the (household) gods' at the doorpost — Vulgate diis, some scholars on ancient Near Eastern analogies.

question: her children come out alive (premature birth) or miscarry
verdict: open; a premature live birth is slightly favoured
context: Yatsa' is used of live birth (Gen 25:25-26) and yeladim of living children, and 'no harm' follows the birth; but whether the 'ason of vv. 22-23 refers to the mother, the child or both is not stated. The literal rendering keeps the question open, as the KJV's 'her fruit depart' also does. Other possible meanings: (1) 'she miscarries', with the harm of v. 23 concerning the mother — LXX (penalty depending on whether the foetus was formed), Philo, Mekhilta, NRSV, NJPS; (2) 'she gives birth prematurely', so that v. 23 covers harm to mother or child — NIV, NASB, CSB, NET.

question: revile God, or revile the gods / judges
context: Elohim with a singular sense is normal, and the pairing with the human chief (nasi) sets divine and human authority side by side. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS, CSB and NET read 'God'. Acts 23:5 quotes only the second line. Other possible meanings: (1) 'the gods' (do not revile other peoples' gods) — LXX theous, Vulgate diis, Philo, Josephus, KJV; (2) 'the judges' — Targum Onkelos (dayyana), Mekhilta, Rashi, cf. 21:6.

question: badgers' skins, or a fine leather
context: Tachash is uncertain. It was a valued material (Ezek 16:10, luxury sandals), not a badger's pelt; proposals include an Egyptian loanword for fine or dyed leather and Arabic tuhas 'dolphin/dugong'. 'Fine leather' (NRSV, NET; NIV 'durable leather') commits least to a species. Other possible meanings: (1) sea-cow/dugong or dolphin/porpoise skins — NJPS 'dolphin skins', NASB95 'porpoise skins', NIV 1984 'sea cows'; (2) violet/blue-dyed skins — LXX hyakinthina, Vulgate ianthina; (3) goatskins — ESV; (4) 'badgers' skins' — KJV, from a Talmudic identification of tachash as an animal.

question: for Azazel (name) or for the scapegoat
context: The two lots are 'one for Yahweh and one for Azazel': the parallel requires a recipient, so Azazel is a name, as ESV, NRSV, NJPS and NET render it. What Azazel denotes (a wilderness being, a place, or 'removal') is left open by keeping the name. Other possible meanings: (1) 'for the scapegoat / the goat that departs' ('ez 'azal) — LXX to apopompaio, Vulgate caper emissarius, KJV, NIV, NASB; (2) 'for (complete) removal' — some lexicons (BDB); (3) a rugged cliff in the wilderness — Talmud (Yoma 67b), Rashi; (4) a demon or fallen angel — 1 Enoch 8-10, many modern scholars.

question: atonement for the soul, or by means of the life
context: The verse grounds atonement in the fact that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood'; be- is most naturally instrumental, 'by means of the life' (ESV, NASB, NET), and avoids merely repeating 'for your lives'. A beth of price ('in exchange for life') is also seriously argued. Other possible meanings: (1) 'in exchange for the life' (life for life) — LXX anti psyches, several commentators; (2) 'as life' (the blood, being life, atones) — NRSV, NJPS; (3) 'for the soul/life' — Vulgate pro animae, KJV, NIV.

question: she shall be scourged, or there shall be an inquiry / compensation
context: Biqqoret is a hapax from baqar 'examine, seek'; 'inquiry' (LXX episkope, NRSV) stays closest to the root, while Akkadian baqaru 'claim' supports 'compensation'. No death penalty and the guilt offering (19:21) rule out a capital sentence, but translations divide three ways; confidence lowered. Nothing in the word singles out the woman. Other possible meanings: (1) 'there shall be compensation/an indemnity' — NJPS, NET, Speiser, Milgrom; (2) 'there shall be punishment' — NIV, NASB, CSB; Vulgate vapulabunt ambo ('both shall be beaten'); (3) 'a distinction shall be made' (from adultery with a free woman) — ESV; (4) 'she shall be scourged' — Sifra, Talmud (Keritot 11a), KJV.

question: as a chief man, or as a husband
verdict: as a husband (i.e. not for in-laws)
context: Ba'al most often means 'husband' or 'owner'; after 21:1-3 lists the blood relatives a priest may mourn, 21:4 most naturally excludes kin by marriage. ESV, NRSV and NET read 'as a husband'; NIV, NASB, NJPS and CSB 'for relatives by marriage'. The terse Hebrew may be damaged. Other possible meanings: (1) 'being a chief man among his people' — Vulgate (in principe), KJV, a sense of ba'al not otherwise attested; (2) not even for his own wife — some interpreters, while rabbinic tradition (Sifra) limits it to a wife unfit for him; (3) emended to refer to a married sister (cf. 21:3) — some critical scholars.

question: a person under the ban put to death, or a person vowed
verdict: a person under the ban of destruction
context: Cherem of persons denotes those placed under the ban of destruction, in war (1 Sam 15) or by judicial sentence (Exod 22:19). Since 27:1-8 lets vowed persons be redeemed, 27:29 is best read of persons already under the ban, not private vows. The rendering follows the Hebrew closely, as ESV and NRSV do. Other possible meanings: (1) a person devoted to God by an individual's vow must die — read by some into the Jephthah story (Judg 11:30-39), but most reject it since 27:1-8 provides redemption; (2) a person already condemned to death by a court cannot be valued or ransomed — Mishnah Arakhin, Rashi.

question: badgers' skins, or a fine leather
context: As Exod 39:34: tachash is uncertain but denotes a valued material (Ezek 16:10), not a badger's pelt. 'Fine leather' (NRSV, NET; NIV 'durable leather') commits least to a species. Other possible meanings: (1) sea-cow/dugong or dolphin/porpoise skins — NJPS 'dolphin skins', NASB95 'porpoise skins', NIV 1984 'sea cows'; (2) violet/blue-dyed skins — LXX hyakinthina, Vulgate ianthina; (3) goatskins — ESV; (4) 'badgers' skins' — KJV, from a Talmudic identification of tachash as an animal.

question: see when covered, or look even for an instant
context: 4:15-19 forbid the Kohathites to touch or see the holy things; kevalla' 'as a swallowing' is best taken as an idiom for an instant (cf. Job 7:19 'till I swallow my spit'), as ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV and CSB render. The Targum and Vulgate instead relate it to the wrapping of the objects. Other possible meanings: (1) 'when the holy things are covered/wrapped' (bala' 'swallow up, envelop') — Targum Onkelos, Vulgate, Rashi, KJV; (2) 'witness the dismantling of the sanctuary' (bala' 'take down') — NJPS; (3) 'suddenly' — LXX exapina.

question: giants, or the Nephilim
context: Nephilim is a proper term (Gen 6:4) of uncertain meaning; transliterating it, as ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS and CSB do, keeps it open, while the grasshopper comparison shows the spies meant men of huge size. The parenthesis linking Anakim to Nephilim is absent from the LXX and may be a gloss. Other possible meanings: (1) 'giants' — LXX and Vulgate gigantes, KJV; (2) 'fallen ones', from naphal 'fall' — some Jewish interpreters (cf. Rashi on Gen 6:4); (3) the parenthesis as a later scribal note rather than part of the spies' speech — many commentators, since the LXX lacks it.

question: what he did at the Red Sea, or the places Waheb in Suphah
context: The object marker 'et with no verb shows a quoted fragment. Waheb and Suphah are best taken as places, matching 'the wadis of the Arnon' and the itinerary of 21:10-20. ESV, NASB, NRSV and NJPS read 'Waheb in Suphah'; NIV 'Zahab in Suphah'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'what he did at the Red Sea' (Suphah taken as Yam Suph) — Targum, Rashi, Vulgate (sicut fecit in mari Rubro), KJV; (2) 'he set Zoob on fire', reading a verb — LXX; (3) 'Zahab' rather than 'Waheb' — NIV, following some versional evidence.

question: unicorn, or wild ox
context: Re'em is the wild ox or aurochs (Akkadian rimu), a two-horned beast: Deut 33:17 speaks of the horns (plural) of a re'em. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS and CSB all read 'wild ox'. To'afot is less certain: 'horns' (ESV, NRSV, NJPS) or 'strength' (NIV). Other possible meanings: (1) 'unicorn', a one-horned beast — LXX monokeros, KJV; Vulgate 'rhinoceros'; (2) 'strength' or 'towering might' rather than 'horns' for to'afot — LXX doxa, Vulgate fortitudo, KJV, NIV.

question: if you turn (condition), or you will return (prediction)
context: The waw-perfects ve-shavta, ve-shama'ta continue the future of 4:29 ('you will seek ... you will find'), and 30:1-3 predicts the same return in exile. LXX reads a future. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV and NJPS all render a prediction. Other possible meanings: (1) a condition, 'if you turn to Yahweh your God and obey his voice' — KJV, Geneva; a waw-perfect after a temporal clause can carry conditional force; (2) an exhortation, 'then return to Yahweh your God' — some commentators.

question: Yahweh is one, or Yahweh alone
verdict: Yahweh our God, Yahweh is one (parsing left open)
context: A verbless clause. 'Echad normally means 'one' ('alone' is usually levad), and LXX kyrios heis estin and Mark 12:29-32 read 'one'. Leaving the first half verbless, as ESV, NIV and CSB do, keeps open both 'Yahweh our God is one Yahweh' and 'Yahweh is our God, Yahweh is one/alone'; 6:5 and 6:14-15 stress exclusive loyalty. Other possible meanings: (1) 'Yahweh is our God, Yahweh alone' — NRSV/NRSVue, NJPS, many commentators ('echad as 'only', cf. 1 Chr 29:1; Zech 14:9); (2) 'Yahweh our God is one Yahweh' — LXX, Mark 12:29, KJV, ESV/NIV notes; (3) 'Yahweh is our God; Yahweh is one', two clauses stressing his unity — NASB, NET.

question: bastard, or one born of a forbidden union
verdict: one born of a forbidden union
context: Mamzer occurs only here and Zech 9:6. Rabbinic law (m. Yevamot 4:13) takes it as the child of incest or adultery; the LXX has 'son of a harlot'. 'Forbidden union' (ESV; NIV, NRSV similar) covers these without the English sense of any child born out of wedlock. The precise reference stays uncertain. Other possible meanings: (1) 'child of a prostitute' — LXX ek pornes, Vulgate de scorto natus; (2) 'bastard', a child born outside marriage — KJV, NASB 'of illegitimate birth'; (3) a person of mixed or foreign descent — some commentators from Zech 9:6 and the following ban on Ammonites and Moabites; NJPS 'misbegotten' leaves it open.

question: a perishing Aramean, or a wandering Aramean
context: 'Oved means 'perishing, lost, straying' (of strayed animals, Deut 22:3; Jer 50:6). With 'he went down to Egypt and lived there as a foreigner' it describes Jacob as a homeless, endangered migrant. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV and CSB read 'wandering', NJPS 'fugitive'; 'wandering' loses some of the sense of danger. Other possible meanings: (1) 'ready to perish' or 'starving' — KJV, several lexicons and medieval commentators (Ibn Ezra); (2) 'an Aramean (Laban) sought to destroy my father', reading 'oved as causative — Targum Onqelos, the Passover Haggadah, Rashi, Vulgate (persequebatur); (3) 'fugitive' — NJPS.

question: for the avenging of Israel, or when the leaders led / let hair loose
verdict: when the leaders took the lead
context: Para' means 'let loose (hair)'; pera'ot is either 'leaders' (cf. Arabic far' 'top, chief'; LXX(A) 'when leaders led'; 5:9 'the commanders of Israel') or 'loose locks' of warriors under a vow (cf. Deut 32:42). The parallel 'people offered themselves' suits either. ESV, NIV, NASB and CSB read 'leaders'; NRSV and NJPS 'locks'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'when locks hang loose/long in Israel', a war vow — NRSV, NJPS, many commentators (cf. Num 6:5); (2) 'for the avenging of Israel', from Aramaic pur'anuta 'retribution' — Targum, Rashi, KJV; (3) 'when a revelation was revealed' — LXX(B).

question: mountains melted, or quaked
context: MT points nazelu 'flowed' (nazal), but the same consonants read nazollu 'quaked' (zalal), as LXX esaleuthesan and Isa 63:19 [64:1]; 5:4 describes earthquake and storm. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV and NJPS all read 'quaked'. 'Flowed/melted' with MT's vowels (cf. Mic 1:4; Ps 97:5) stays possible. Zeh sinay is a divine title (cf. Ps 68:9). Other possible meanings: (1) 'the mountains flowed/melted' — MT vocalization, Targum, KJV; (2) 'even this Sinai' or 'that Sinai', a demonstrative pointing to the mountain — KJV, ESV, NASB, rather than the title 'the One of Sinai' (NIV, NRSV, NJPS).

question: nephews, or grandsons
context: Bene banim is literally 'sons of sons', the normal expression for grandchildren (Gen 45:10; Exod 34:7). The Hebrew is not ambiguous; only the English word 'nephew' has shifted meaning. All major modern translations read 'grandsons'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'nephews' — KJV, using 'nephew' in its older sense 'grandson' (Latin nepos), so no real difference of meaning; (2) 'descendants' more broadly — bene banim can extend to later offspring, though nothing here suggests it.

question: gods, or a divine being
context: Saul's follow-up 'What is his appearance?' (singular) and the answer 'an old man is coming up' point to one figure, and elohim can denote a single spirit-being. But the participle 'olim is plural, so she may describe more than one figure, as LXX and Vulgate read. NASB, NRSV and NJPS read 'a divine being'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'gods' or 'divine beings coming up', more than one figure — LXX theous, Vulgate deos, KJV, some commentators from the plural participle; (2) 'a god' — ESV; (3) 'a ghostly figure' or 'spirit form', the dead as elohim (cf. Isa 8:19) — NIV, CSB.

question: teach the use of the bow, or teach 'The Bow' (a title)
context: Qeshet stands with no verb or article right after 'to teach the sons of Judah', and the lament follows at once; nothing concerns archery, though 1:22 mentions Jonathan's bow, which may explain the title. NIV, NASB, NRSV and NJPS take it as the song's name. Other possible meanings: (1) 'teach the sons of Judah [the use of] the bow', archery training — Targum, Rashi, KJV; (2) 'bow' as a scribal intrusion or obscure musical term — the LXX (B) lacks the word and some commentators delete or emend it.

question: Elhanan killed Goliath, or the brother of Goliath
context: MT and LXX both read 'Goliath'. The text is visibly disturbed ('oregim, 'weavers', seems copied from the line's end), and 1 Chr 20:5 may preserve an original 'Lahmi the brother of Goliath'; but no witness to Samuel reads that, so the translation keeps the source and leaves the tension with 1 Sam 17 (ESV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS, CSB do the same). Other possible meanings: (1) '[the brother of] Goliath', supplied from 1 Chr 20:5 — KJV, NIV, NET; many think Chronicles reflects the better text; (2) Elhanan as another name for David — Targum and some rabbinic and later commentators; (3) a second Philistine named Goliath, or 'Goliath' as a title — some conservative commentators.

question: his ascent to the house of Yahweh, or the burnt offerings he offered
context: 'Olah elsewhere always means burnt offering, and 'olah with the causative of 'alah is the standard idiom 'offer a burnt offering'. LXX and Vulgate read offerings here, the LXX also at 2 Chr 9:4. ESV, NIV, NRSV, NJPS and CSB read offerings. MT 2 Chr 9:4 'aliyyato 'his ascent' supports the alternative. Other possible meanings: (1) 'his ascent (stairway) by which he went up to the house of Yahweh' — MT 2 Chr 9:4, KJV, NASB (1995); (2) 'his upper chamber' at the temple — some commentators reading 'aliyyah literally in Chronicles.

question: went up against, or went up to (help) the king of Assyria
verdict: went up to the king of Assyria
context: 'Alah 'al often means 'go up against', but 'al can mean 'to/toward' (as 'el), and the Babylonian Chronicle shows Neco marched in 609 BC to support Assyria at Harran against Babylon. ESV, NASB, NRSV and CSB read 'to'; NIV 'to help'. 2 Chr 35:20 gives Carchemish as his goal. Other possible meanings: (1) 'went up against the king of Assyria' — KJV, the commoner sense of 'alah 'al; Josephus (Ant. 10.74) has Neco marching against the Medes and Babylonians, and some take 'king of Assyria' as whoever then ruled Assyria (Babylon); (2) 'went up on behalf of' ('al = for) — some commentators.

question: you regard me as a man of high degree, or shown me future generations
verdict: you regard me as a man of high rank
context: MT ur'itani is the plain stem 'you have seen/regarded me', not 'shown me'; tor 'turn, rank' (Esth 2:12) with hamma'alah 'high' gives 'regarded me as a man of high rank', as NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS and CSB read (agreeing in substance with the KJV). The phrase is obscure and 2 Sam 7:19 differs; the text may be damaged. Other possible meanings: (1) 'you have shown me future generations' — ESV, emending tor to dor 'generation' and reading the verb as causative; (2) 'this is the instruction (torah) for mankind' — the parallel 2 Sam 7:19; (3) 'you looked on me as a man's vision and exalted me' — LXX; (4) 'you have seen me as a man of the line going upward' — literal renderings.
rendering_changed: yes (flag removed: now agrees with the KJV)

question: Satan, or an adversary
context: Satan without the article (contrast 'the satan' in Job 1-2 and Zech 3) behaves like a proper name; the figure incites the king where 2 Sam 24:1 has Yahweh's anger, a known theological shift in Chronicles, and no human adversary appears in the story. LXX diabolos. ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS and CSB read 'Satan'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'an adversary', a human enemy whose threat prompted the census — NET ('An adversary opposed Israel'), Sara Japhet and other scholars, cf. satan indefinite in 1 Kgs 11:14, 23; (2) 'an accuser', an unnamed heavenly prosecutor like the satan of Job — some commentators.

question: yet will I trust in him (qere), or I have no hope (ketiv)
context: WLC has ketiv lo' 'not' and qere lo 'for him'. The qere is the Masoretic reading tradition, followed by Targum and Vulgate (in ipso sperabo) and by ESV, NIV, NASB, CSB and NET; 13:16 'this will be my salvation' fits hope. The ketiv fits 13:14 and 'yet I will argue'. Genuinely balanced. Other possible meanings: (1) 'Behold, he will kill me; I have no hope' (ketiv lo') — NRSV, NJPS, many commentators (Pope, Clines), Job defiant in despair; (2) 'I will not hold back/wait', i.e. I will speak regardless — some commentators; (3) a quite different text — LXX ('even if the Mighty One lays hands on me').

question: in my flesh, or apart from my flesh
verdict: 'from my flesh' (ambiguity kept; most read embodied sight)
context: 'From my flesh' keeps the Hebrew min open: 'from within' (embodied sight, supported by 19:27 'my eyes shall behold, and not another') or 'apart from'. ESV, NIV, NRSV, NJPS and CSB render 'in my flesh'; NASB 'from my flesh'. Whether Job means after death, resurrection, or vindication before death stays open. Other possible meanings: (1) 'without/apart from my flesh', seeing God after death — RSV, ESV/NIV/NRSV footnotes, many critical commentators; (2) 'in my flesh', bodily resurrection — Vulgate (in carne mea), KJV, traditional Christian reading; (3) 'while still in my flesh', before death — NJPS.

question: I abhor myself and repent, or I retract and am comforted
verdict: I reject my words and repent
context: 'Em'as has no object: 42:3 ('I spoke what I did not understand') favours rejecting his words, though 'despise myself' (LXX, Vulgate) is equally defensible. Nicham 'al most naturally means 'repent/relent' here (ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS, CSB, NET); 'be consoled' (Targum) is a minority reading. Whether he repents of sin or of his lawsuit stays open; 42:7 affirms Job. Other possible meanings: (1) 'I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes' — LXX, Vulgate, KJV, ESV, NIV, NRSV, NET; (2) 'I recant and relent, being but dust and ashes' (creaturely humility, cf. Gen 18:27) — NJPS, CSB; (3) 'I am consoled concerning dust and ashes' or 'I repent of dust and ashes' (cease mourning) — Targum, some modern commentators; (4) 'I melt away' — LXX etaken, some scholars.

question: blesses the greedy and renounces Yahweh, or the greedy curses and renounces Yahweh
verdict: the greedy man curses and renounces Yahweh
context: Ni'ets with God as object recurs in 10:13 ('why does the wicked renounce God?'), so 'renounces Yahweh' is secure. Barakh is unsettled: 'curses' (scribal euphemism, as Job 1:5; 1 Kgs 21:10) with the greedy man as subject (ESV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS), or the wicked 'blesses the greedy' (NIV, CSB, NET). Other possible meanings: (1) 'he blesses the greedy and spurns Yahweh' — NIV, CSB, NET; (2) 'the greedy man blesses himself', i.e. boasts — some commentators; (3) 'blesses the covetous, whom Yahweh abhors', Yahweh as subject — KJV (less likely given 10:13); (4) 'the unjust man is blessed' — LXX, Vulgate.

question: they pierced (versions), or like a lion (MT)
verdict: they pierce (ancient versions, against MT 'like a lion')
context: Here the CT departs from WLC ka'ari 'like a lion', which leaves the line without a verb. A verb is read by the LXX (oryxan 'they dug'), Peshitta, Vulgate, the Nahal Hever psalms scroll (k'rw) and some Masoretic manuscripts; ESV, NIV, NASB and CSB follow it. The verb's exact sense (dig, pierce, bind) is uncertain. Other possible meanings: (1) 'like a lion [they are at / maul] my hands and my feet' — MT, Targum (conflating), NJPS, NET, many critical scholars, fitting the beast pattern of vv.13-14, 21-22; (2) 'they bind my hands and my feet' — Aquila, Symmachus, Jerome's Hebrew Psalter (vinxerunt); (3) 'my hands and feet have shriveled' — NRSV.
rendering_changed: yes (flag removed: now agrees with the KJV)

question: O congregation (or silence), or you gods / mighty ones
verdict: you gods ('elim: rulers or divine beings)
context: MT 'elem 'silence' scarcely works as an address; nearly all modern versions read the same consonants as 'elim 'gods, mighty ones'. 'Your hands deal out violence on earth' (v. 3) and Ps 82 point to powers who judge; whether they are human rulers or heavenly beings is left open by 'you gods'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'O congregation' — KJV, taking 'elem as 'band, assembly'; (2) 'you silent ones' / 'in silence' — MT vowels, Rashi, NKJV; (3) 'you rulers / mighty ones' (human leaders) — NIV, NET, CSB, NJPS; (4) heavenly beings judged as in Ps 82:1, 6 — some commentators.

question: God who created all rewards the fool, or an archer who wounds everyone
verdict: archer image; hires a fool or hires passers-by (MT)
context: Among the most obscure lines in Proverbs. Rab as 'archer' (Jer 50:29) and meholel 'wounding' fits the fool-similes of 26:1-12, as most modern versions take it. The CT now follows the Masoretic text ('hires ... hires') instead of repointing the second soker as shikkor 'drunkard', which no ancient witness requires. Other possible meanings: (1) 'The great God who formed all things rewards the fool and rewards transgressors' — KJV, some medieval Jewish readings (rab = God); (2) 'A master produces everything, but one who hires a fool ...' — NJPS (rab = master craftsman); (3) 'a passing fool or drunkard' — ESV, NRSV, repointing shikkor; (4) the LXX has an entirely different line about the flesh of fools suffering.

question: names (Ithiel, Ucal), or 'I am weary, O God'
verdict: I am weary, O God ... and worn out (revocalised)
context: The consonants allow names (MT vowels: 'to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal') or a confession, la'iti 'el ... wa'ekel 'I am weary, O God ... and worn out'. The confession fits vv. 2-3 and explains the doubled phrase but needs new vowels; major versions divide almost evenly, so the CT keeps it with low confidence. Other possible meanings: (1) personal names 'to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal' — MT vowels, KJV, NASB, NJPS, CSB, NET; (2) 'I am weary, O God ... how can I prevail?' / 'but I can prevail' (we'ukal 'I am able') — NRSV, NIV; (3) 'There is no God ... and I am helpless' — some commentators; (4) Vulgate interprets the names: 'the man with whom God is, who was strengthened'.

question: musical instruments, or concubines
context: Shiddah weshiddot occurs only here. Placed after male and female singers and 'the delights of the sons of man', 'a woman and women', i.e. a harem, suits a king's catalogue (cf. 1 Kgs 11:3) and is followed by most modern versions; but the etymology is uncertain and the ancient versions each guess differently. Other possible meanings: (1) 'musical instruments, and that of all sorts' — KJV, following some medieval Jewish commentators; (2) 'male and female cupbearers' — LXX; (3) 'cups and pitchers for pouring wine' — Vulgate; (4) 'chests, coffers' (Mishnaic shiddah) — NJPS 'coffers and coffers of them'; (5) baths and bathhouses — Targum.

question: the spirit goes up (statement), or whether it goes up (question)
verdict: a question: who knows whether ... whether
context: The consonants allow the interrogative ha- 'whether', read by the LXX (ei), Vulgate (si) and most modern versions and suiting the doubt of 3:19-22. But MT points it as the article ('that goes up'), and 12:7 'the spirit returns to God' shows the book does not deny an ascent, so the question is favoured, not certain. Other possible meanings: (1) 'Who knows the spirit of man that goes upward, and the spirit of the beast that goes down?' — MT vowels, KJV, NASB, NKJV, much Jewish tradition, implying that man's spirit does rise; (2) the question read as a denial ('no one knows that it rises') rather than as honest uncertainty — some commentators.

question: a virgin will conceive, or the young woman is pregnant
verdict: the young woman is pregnant (a sign in Ahaz's time)
context: 'Almah is a young woman of marriageable age (Gen 24:43; Exod 2:8), not the specific word for virgin (betulah); Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion render neanis. Harah is an adjective, 'pregnant', and v. 16 sets the sign within a few years. But harah can look forward (Judg 13:5), and the major versions divide, so this is favoured rather than certain. Other possible meanings: (1) 'the/a virgin shall conceive' — LXX parthenos, Vulgate virgo, Matt 1:23, KJV, ESV, NIV, NASB, CSB, holding that 'almah implies an unmarried, chaste girl and that the sign looks to the Messiah; (2) 'the young woman shall conceive / is about to conceive' (future) — RSV, NET; (3) the mother identified as Ahaz's wife or Isaiah's wife (cf. 8:3) — Jewish tradition and many commentators.

question: Lucifer (a name), or Shining One, son of Dawn
verdict: Shining One, son of Dawn (taunt on the king of Babylon)
context: Helel ben-shachar 'shining one, son of dawn' names the morning star (Venus), and 14:4 explicitly makes the song a taunt 'against the king of Babylon'. 'Lucifer' is the Vulgate's Latin word for the morning star, not a Hebrew name. Applying the passage to Satan's fall is a later, secondary interpretation. Other possible meanings: (1) 'Lucifer' as a proper name, applied to Satan — Vulgate lucifer, KJV, Tertullian, Origen and much later Christian tradition (cf. Luke 10:18); (2) 'Day Star / morning star' — LXX heosphoros, ESV, NRSV, NIV, NASB, CSB; (3) 'Howl!' (helel from yalal, as in Zech 11:2) — Peshitta and some ancient Jewish readers.

question: scattered and peeled, or tall and smooth
verdict: tall and smooth; mighty and conquering
context: Memushshak umorat most naturally means 'drawn out (tall) and polished (smooth)', fitting Cush (18:1; cf. Herodotus 3.20 on the tall Ethiopians) and the 'feared' people of the next line; the LXX's 'lofty nation' agrees. Qaw-qaw umebusah is obscure, and 'mighty and conquering' is a reasonable guess among several. Other possible meanings: (1) 'scattered and peeled ... meted out and trodden down' — KJV, making the people victims; (2) 'a nation of strange speech' / 'gibber and chatter' for qaw-qaw (cf. 28:10) — NIV, NJPS; (3) 'far and remote, thrust forth and away' — NJPS; (4) 'a lofty nation, a strange and harsh people' — LXX.

question: precept upon precept, or mocking babble
context: Vv. 9-10 quote scoffers mocking the prophet as if he taught infants; v. 11 answers with 'stammering lips and a foreign tongue', and v. 13 turns the same syllables into judgment. Many scholars hear childish or nonsense syllables, but tsav and qav are real words and most major versions translate them; transliteration keeps both open. Other possible meanings: (1) 'precept upon precept, line upon line' — KJV, ESV, NRSV, NASB, CSB 'law after law', mocking the prophet's elementary lessons; (2) 'Do this, do that, a rule for this, a rule for that' — NIV; (3) 'mutter upon mutter' / meaningless gibberish — NJPS, NET; (4) 'affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope' — LXX; 'command, command again; wait, wait again' — Vulgate.

question: until he comes whose right it is (messianic), or to whom judgment is given
verdict: literal 'the one to whom judgment belongs'; referent left open
context: Mishpat can mean 'judgment' or 'right, due' (Deut 21:17; Jer 32:8), and the line echoes Gen 49:10. It may mean Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God commits judgment (cf. 23:24), or the rightful Davidic king for whom the crown waits (cf. 34:23-24; 37:24). The LXX and most versions take 'right'. The literal English leaves both open. Other possible meanings: (1) 'until he comes whose right it is' — the rightful (messianic) king; LXX 'to whom it belongs', KJV, NASB, NRSV, NIV, NJPS, much Jewish and Christian exegesis; (2) 'the one to whom I have assigned the judgment' — Babylon's king as God's agent; NET, W. L. Moran and many commentators.

question: you shall take your inheritance in yourself, or be profaned by your own doing
verdict: you shall be profaned (Niphal of halal)
context: Venihalt is best taken as the Niphal of halal 'be profaned', as in 7:24 (venihalu) and 22:26, matching the shame of exile in 22:15; most modern versions agree. The ancient versions derive it from nahal 'inherit, possess', mostly with God as subject, so another sense remains possible. Other possible meanings: (1) 'you shall take your inheritance in yourself' — KJV (nahal); (2) 'I will take possession of you' — LXX, Vulgate (possidebo), reading a first-person verb from nahal; (3) 'I shall be profaned through you' — NRSV, first person with halal (cf. 20:9, 14).

question: 69 weeks to the Messiah, or 7 weeks to an anointed prince, then 62 weeks of rebuilding
verdict: seven weeks to an anointed prince; then sixty-two weeks of rebuilding (MT accents)
context: The WLC's atnach divides after 'seven weeks', 'an anointed one, a prince' lacks the article, and 9:26 places an anointed one 'cut off' after the 62 weeks, suggesting two figures. But Theodotion and the Vulgate join both numbers to the anointed one, the accents are mediaeval, and major versions split. The CT follows its source's accents with low confidence. Other possible meanings: (1) 'unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks' (69 weeks to the Messiah) — Theodotion, Vulgate, KJV, NIV, NASB, CSB, NET, the classic Christian chronology ending in Jesus; (2) the anointed one after seven weeks as Cyrus (Isa 45:1), Zerubbabel or Joshua the high priest — commentators following the accents, cf. ESV, NRSV, NJPS.

question: I (God) hate divorce, or the man who hates and divorces
verdict: the man who hates and divorces covers his garment with violence
context: Sane' is third person ('one hating'), not 'I hate', and the LXX, 4QXIIa, Targum and Vulgate all make the husband the subject. This continues 2:14-15 and fits the closing 'do not be faithless'. Yet a divine statement 'I hate divorce' is widely held, and the syntax is difficult. Other possible meanings: (1) 'For I hate divorce / he hates divorce, says Yahweh' — KJV, NASB, NRSV, NJPS, NET, as God's own attitude; (2) 'if you hate her, divorce her' (permission, cf. Deut 24:1) — 4QXIIa, Targum, Vulgate, LXX 'if you hate and send away'; (3) 'covers violence with his garment' — KJV, reversing the image.

question: Barabbas, or Jesus Barabbas
context: SBLGNT reads Iesoun Barabban in 27:16-17 with Theta, family 1 and copies known to Origen, who disliked giving the name Jesus to a sinner; omission out of reverence is easier to explain than insertion, and Pilate's choice between two men called Jesus gains point. But the supporting witnesses are few, and NA28 brackets the name. Other possible meanings: (1) 'a notable prisoner, called Barabbas' — TR/Majority text, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus (whose 'ton Barabban' in 27:17 may preserve a trace of the name), most manuscripts, KJV, ESV, NASB, CSB. 'Jesus Barabbas' is read by NIV, NRSV and NET.

question: moved with compassion, or moved with anger
context: SBLGNT adopts orgistheis (Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts) as the harder reading: scribes would soften anger to compassion more readily than the reverse, and Matthew and Luke both omit the emotion here. 1:43 'sternly charged him' fits. But nearly all manuscripts read splanchnistheis, and NA28 prints it. Other possible meanings: (1) 'moved with compassion/pity' — splanchnistheis, TR/Majority, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, A, most manuscripts and versions, NA28, KJV, ESV, NASB, CSB; (2) anger directed at the disease and its effects rather than at the man — NIV 'indignant', NET 'indignation' and commentators who adopt orgistheis.

question: is 16:9-20 original?
verdict: a later addition, kept in double brackets
context: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end at 16:8; Clement and Origen show no knowledge of 16:9-20; Eusebius and Jerome report it missing from most copies they knew; and its vocabulary, style and abrupt reintroduction of Mary Magdalene (named in 16:1) differ from Mark. Most scholars and SBLGNT judge it an early second-century addition. Other possible meanings: (1) the authentic conclusion of Mark — TR/Majority, A, C, D, W and the great majority of manuscripts, Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.10.5 cites 16:19), Tatian; KJV, NKJV and defenders such as Burgon, Lunn and Snapp; (2) the Shorter Ending — L, Psi and a few others; (3) Mark's true ending was lost after 16:8 rather than meant to stop there — some scholars.

question: is 'Father, forgive them' original?
verdict: uncertain; printed in double brackets with SBLGNT
context: Strong early witnesses omit the prayer (P75, Vaticanus, D*, W, Theta), but Sinaiticus*, A, C, L, most manuscripts and early Fathers include it; its Lukan style (prayer to 'Father', 23:46; cf. Acts 7:60) supports authenticity, and deliberate omission is conceivable. The brackets mark doubt, not rejection. Other possible meanings: (1) authentic Luke, printed without marks — TR/Majority, Sinaiticus*, A, C, L, Irenaeus (Latin), KJV, and in the text of ESV, NIV, NRSV and NET with footnotes; (2) an authentic saying of Jesus from oral tradition but not part of Luke's text — Westcott and Hort; (3) a later addition modelled on Acts 7:60 — some textual critics.

question: is the woman taken in adultery original?
verdict: a later addition, kept in double brackets
context: 7:53-8:11 is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, W and the earliest versions; no Greek Father comments on it before the 12th century; its vocabulary is Lukan; and manuscripts place it variously (after John 7:36, 7:44 or 21:25, or Luke 21:38). 7:52 flows into 8:12. Most scholars see an old, possibly genuine story, not John's text. Other possible meanings: (1) part of John's original Gospel — TR/Majority (from Codex D, c. 400, onward), Vulgate (Jerome included it), Augustine, who thought some removed it for fear of moral laxity; KJV, NKJV; (2) an early, authentic story about Jesus later inserted into John — Papias (via Eusebius), the Didascalia, most scholars; printed bracketed in ESV, NIV, NASB, CSB.

question: the heavenly witnesses, or three that testify
verdict: three that testify: the Spirit, the water and the blood (no Comma)
context: The heavenly witnesses appear in no Greek manuscript before about the 14th century (629, 61, 918, 2318 and a few margins), in no early version, and in no Greek Father during the Trinitarian debates; they arose in Latin sources (Priscillian, c. 380) and entered later Vulgate copies. 5:6 and 5:8 carry the Spirit-water-blood argument. Other possible meanings: (1) 'three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one' — TR (Erasmus 1522 onward), KJV, later Vulgate manuscripts, perhaps Cyprian (De unitate 6); the Byzantine Majority Text lacks it; (2) the Spirit, water and blood read as baptism, the cross and the eucharist — an interpretation of the shorter text.

question: do his commandments, or wash their robes
context: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Vulgate read 'wash their robes', echoing 7:14. The Byzantine 'do his commandments' looks similar in uncial script (PLYNONTESTASSTOLAS / POIOUNTESTASENTOLAS) and may have been drawn to 12:17 and 14:12. The earlier witnesses and the book's own imagery favour 'wash'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'those who do his commandments' — TR, most Byzantine manuscripts (046), Tertullian, Cyprian, KJV, NKJV, cf. Rev 12:17; 14:12; (2) the washing understood specifically of baptism or of martyrdom (cf. 7:14) — various commentators.

question: book of life, or tree of life
context: Every Greek manuscript reads xylou 'tree' of life, as does the Vulgate (ligno); 'book' (libro) is a Latin copying slip. Erasmus, whose Greek manuscript lacked the end of Revelation, back-translated from Latin and so brought 'book of life' into the TR. 22:2 and 22:14 confirm 'tree'. Other possible meanings: (1) 'God shall take away his part out of the book of life' — TR, KJV, NKJV, some Latin manuscripts and Latin writers, echoing 3:5 and 20:15 where the book of life appears; the Majority Text reads 'tree'.
